items.body: @AngewisnolongerproudofSO I don't see a reason to mention that specifically. Discarding and redoing procedural results which are undesirable (for whatever reason - not just profanity but also simply because they would result in a bad or imbalanced game experience) and can be detected automatically should be part of your procedural generation algorithms. And when you discover one unique result people complain about but which is unlikely to occur a 2nd time, you would fix that by replacing that part of the world manually, which will give you a "part of the galaxy which you designed by hand".

items.body: From what I once read about Elite&co's procedural generation, there's one more bullet point for your "store explicitly" list: a list of exceptions where the procedural results should be discarded because they happen to generate inappropriate content (NSFW system names etc.)
Take a look at this video, it explains the concepts in Philipp answer in a very simple and very clear way: youtube.com/watch?v=ZZY9YE7rZJw

This is a great answer and very helpful. I am already in the process of learning how to apply Procedural Generation. I think it's indeed a better way to do all of this, and allows me to easily have multiple galaxies with way more solar systems. As of the monotony problem - I already have a possible solution for that. A mix of random factors making solar systems quasi-unique as they peak, and presets that set up a special constellation at baseline, like a resource rich planet dangerously close to a star, or a star emitting excessive amounts of lethal solar flares.

According to this, the Frontier team started with the 160,000 known star systems and then uses a system they developed called Stellar Forge to generate the rest based on first principles of astrophysics theory.
No Man's Sky was infamous for overuse of procedurally generated content resulting in overly repetitive gameplay.

Now I want to implement a galaxy generator like that. But I must restrain myself. Starting your game project by making a procedural generation system when you didn't create the actual game yet is a bad idea. You won't yet know what content your game actually needs. And when you don't know that, then your procedural generation will end up creating plenty of content which doesn't actually do much to help the game mechanics to shine and instead just result in a bland and boring game experience. Elite:Dangerous suffered a lot from that.
